🧰 Make-Do Household Guide How to make or replace everyday necessities when the store is gone — from basic supplies, things you can scavenge, and what grows around the Illinois Valley. Each section points to the detailed manuals in Homestead-Skills\ (especially Household-Make-Do\, Soap-Candles\ and Sanitation-Water\) and Electronics-Repair\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never mix cleaning chemicals. Bleach + ammonia (or urine) makes toxic chloramine gas; bleach + vinegar or any acid makes chlorine gas. Use one product, rinse, then the next. - Lye (from ashes or the store) burns skin and blinds. Gloves and eye protection; flush any splash with plenty of water for 15 minutes. Never use aluminum pots with lye. - Label every container. Never store chemicals or fuel in food or drink bottles, and never reuse a container that held chemicals or fuel for food or water. - Never put gasoline in a lamp, stove or heater, and never burn charcoal, a camp stove or a generator indoors (carbon monoxide).

🧽 Cleaning and disinfecting - Most cleaning is just soap, hot water and scrubbing — it removes most germs along with the dirt. Homemade lye soap works fine (Soap-Candles\). - Scouring powder: baking soda, fine wood ash, or fine sand on a damp rag. - Glass and hard-water film: white vinegar mixed half and half with water (not on marble or stone, and never together with bleach). - Disinfecting with bleach (for kitchen surfaces, sickrooms, after flooding): plain unscented household bleach, 5 tablespoons (⅓ cup) per gallon of water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. Clean first, leave it wet for at least a minute, and mix it fresh every day — diluted bleach loses strength. Drinking water needs a much weaker dose — use the table in Water\EPA - Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water. - No bleach? Boiling water, scrubbing with soap, and drying things in full sun all kill germs.

👕 Laundry - Laundry soap: grate one bar of soap and mix with 1 cup washing soda (add 1 cup borax if you have it). Use 1–2 tablespoons per load, dissolved in hot water first. - Make washing soda from baking soda: spread baking soda in a pan and bake at 400 °F (200 °C) for about an hour, stirring now and then, until it turns dull and grainy. It's stronger than baking soda — wear gloves. - Ash water (old-time "lye wash"): soak hardwood ashes in water, let it settle, and use only the clear liquid for greasy or very dirty clothes. It's caustic — gloves, and never on wool or silk. - Washing by hand: soak overnight, agitate with a clean plunger in a bucket (or a washboard), rinse twice, wring hard, and dry in the sun — sunlight helps disinfect.

🪥 Personal care - Teeth: how you brush matters more than the paste. Brush twice a day with water, a little baking soda, or salt. No brush? Chew the end of a fresh green twig until it frays into bristles. Use thread as floss. (Medical\Manuals-PDF\Where There Is No Dentist) - Deodorant: wash daily; dust on baking soda or cornstarch (baking soda can irritate some skin). - Salve: melt 1 part beeswax with 4 parts oil or clean tallow (by weight) over low heat and pour into small tins. Lip balm is firmer: about 1 part wax to 2 parts oil. - Hair: wash with soap, then rinse with a cup of water with a spoonful of vinegar in it to remove soap film.

🩲 Menstrual pads and diapers - Reusable pads: several layers of absorbent cotton (old flannel or towel) sewn or folded into a pad, held in underwear. Rinse in cold water first, wash with soap, and dry in the sun. See Where Women Have No Doctor (Medical\). - Cloth diapers: absorbent cotton folded in layers, with a wool or plastic cover. Rinse, soak in a lidded bucket, wash hot with soap, dry in the sun.

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives - Water: a squeeze bottle of water, then wash your hands with soap — the cleanest option. - "Family cloth": cotton squares, used once, kept in a lidded bucket and washed hot, separately from other laundry. - Leaves: big soft thimbleberry leaves (common along roads and forest edges here in summer) or first-year mullein leaves. - ⚠️ Learn poison oak first — it's everywhere in the Illinois Valley. Leaves in threes, lobed like small oak leaves, shiny or dull, red in fall. The bare stems in winter still cause the rash. Also avoid stinging nettle.

🔥 Fire and light without stores - Fire starters: cotton balls rubbed with petroleum jelly; fatwood (resin-soaked heartwood from old pine or fir stumps — smells like turpentine and lights even when damp); dry bark and pine pitch. - Char cloth (catches a spark): put squares of 100% cotton cloth in a metal tin with a small nail hole in the lid, set it in a fire until smoke stops coming out, then let it cool before opening. - No matches: a ferro rod or flint-and-steel onto char cloth (steel struck on flint, quartz or pyrite throws sparks); a magnifying glass in sun; touching a 9-volt battery (or two AAs) to fine steel wool; or a bow drill — drill about ⅝ in thick and a foot long, of dry cedar, fir, cottonwood or basswood, on a board of the same wood with a notch cut to the center of the pit; tinder of dry grass with shredded cedar bark (Seton's Book of Woodcraft, pp. 192–194, and the Army survival manuals). - Oil lamp: a glass jar or tin, a wick of twisted cotton string or a cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable oil or melted fat. Keep the flame small. Never gasoline. Tallow candles: Soap-Candles\.

🪵 Glue, patching and waterproofing - Pine pitch glue: gently melt pine resin (it's flammable — heat beside the fire, not in it), stir in powdered charcoal (about 1 part to 3–4 parts resin) plus a pinch of fine plant fiber, and use while warm. Sets hard — for hafting tools, patching containers and seams. - Flour paste: cook flour and water to a thick paste — for paper and labels. - Waterproof cloth or leather: rub in beeswax, tallow or a beeswax–oil mix, then warm it so it soaks in.

👟 Clothing and footwear - Mending: running stitch for seams, backstitch where it must be strong, whipstitch for edges, and darning for holes (weave thread back and forth across the hole, then across the other way). Patch from the inside for strength. Needles from stiff wire; thread from unraveled fabric, dental floss or fishing line. - Sandals from old tires: trace your foot on tire tread, cut with a very sharp knife wetted with soapy water (steel belts make it slow — choose worn tread with no wire showing), sand the edges, and tie on with straps cut from an inner tube or with cord through slots. - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away — avoid it in cold rain.

🔧 Simple plumbing - Dripping faucet: shut the water off first, then replace the washer. A temporary washer can be cut from leather (cold taps) or rubber (hot taps). - Frozen pipe: open the faucet and thaw from the faucet end back toward the supply — never from the middle, where trapped water can burst the pipe. Thaw drains from the low end upward. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs.)

🔌 Electronics: repair and salvage Manuals are in Electronics-Repair\ (and device-by-device guides in the iFixit archive in Kiwix). Start with the Navy safety manual and the Kuphaldt multimeter and soldering guides. Safety first - Unplugged isn't safe. Capacitors hold a charge after unplugging. Discharge them with an insulated tool or shorting probe across the terminals and to the metal chassis, and recheck. - Microwave ovens can kill: the capacitor holds about 2,000 volts. Short it out before touching anything inside, never run the oven with the cover off, and don't break the magnetron's ceramic parts (toxic). Old tube TVs and monitors (CRTs) hold high voltage and can implode — leave them alone unless you know how. - Household 120 V can kill — especially with wet hands. Work with one hand when anything might be live. - Lithium batteries (laptops, phones, tools): throw out any that are swollen, dented, hot, or below about 2.5 volts. Charge only with a proper lithium charger, on a non-flammable surface, never unattended. Finding the fault — check the simple things first: power cord and plug, fuse, switch, batteries and their contacts, loose wires. Then measure voltages, then test parts. Test a part in the circuit before you desolder it. Bulging or leaking capacitors are the most common failure in power supplies and chargers. Multimeter quick tests - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires.

circuit before you desolder it. Bulging or leaking capacitors are the most common failure in power supplies and chargers. Multimeter quick tests - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires. - Diode: conducts one way only — about 0.5–0.7 V on the diode setting forward, nothing backward. Both ways = shorted; neither = open. - Transistor: test it like two diodes back to back (base-emitter, base-collector), and check collector-emitter reads high both ways. - Capacitor (discharged first): on the ohms setting a good one shows a brief "kick" then rising resistance; no kick = open, steady low reading = shorted. Resistor color code: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Bands 1–2 are digits, band 3 is the number of zeros, the last band is tolerance (gold 5%, silver 10%). Example: yellow–violet–orange–gold = 47,000 Ω ±5%. Soldering: use rosin-core solder (never acid-core plumbing solder); a 25-watt iron for circuit boards. Make the wires hold mechanically first, heat the joint, not the solder, and don't move it while it cools. Remove old solder with copper wick or a solder sucker. What to salvage before throwing anything out: - Radios and clock radios: power transformers, cords, switches, knobs, speakers. - Computer power supplies: 12 V and 5 V power, fans, heat sinks, wire, connectors. - Printers and scanners: small

Radios and clock radios: power transformers, cords, switches, knobs, speakers. - Computer power supplies: 12 V and 5 V power, fans, heat sinks, wire, connectors. - Printers and scanners: small motors, gears, rods, belts, switches. - Microwaves (after discharging!): fan and turntable motors, door switches, fuses, magnets. - Cars: batteries, alternators (12 V charging), lights, wire, fuses, relays — see Army TM 9-8000 in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. - Also: LEDs, magnet wire from motors and transformers, fuses, batteries, cords. - Motor run capacitors can be reused; motor start capacitors can burst if used continuously. Crystal radio — no batteries needed (NBS Circular 120, 1922): a long wire antenna (about 75 ft, on insulators), a ground wire to a water pipe (never gas) or a rod in damp soil, a tuning coil wound on an oatmeal box, a germanium diode salvaged from an old radio as the detector, and a high-impedance earphone. It picks up AM stations with no power at all.

🍲 Hay-box cooking (saves fuel) Bring the pot to a full boil, then nest it tightly in hay, wool, newspaper or blankets in a box with a padded lid; it keeps cooking for hours on its own heat. Bring food back to a boil before eating if it has cooled below hot (food is safest kept above 140 °F).

🫙 Containers and storage - Food-grade buckets (recycling number 1 or 2 on the bottom, from bakeries and restaurants), glass jars and metal cans with lids. Wash with soap, then rinse with the bleach solution above. - Keep mice out: metal cans or glass; hang sacks from wire. Set snap traps along walls.

💧 Clean water from plastic bottles (SODIS) Fill clear plastic (PET) bottles of 2 liters or less with clear water, lay them on a roof or shiny surface in full sun for 6 hours (two full days if it's more than half cloudy). Doesn't work with cloudy water — let it settle or filter it first. Details: Sanitation-Water\ and Water\.

🐜 Pests - Roaches and ants: powdered borax mixed with sugar or flour, dusted into cracks (roaches), or a sponge soaked in borax-and-sugar syrup in their trail (ants). Keep borax away from children and pets. - Mosquitoes: screens, netting over beds, and smoke; homemade repellents are weak. - Lice: comb wet hair with a fine-tooth (nit) comb every day for two weeks; wash bedding hot. - Ticks: check every evening, especially after brush; pull straight out with tweezers.For hundreds more recipes — cleaners, polishes, glues, inks, waterproofing, pest control and home remedies — see the classic formula books in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do\. They are old: use their methods, but follow the modern safety rules above, and skip any recipe using mercury (bichloride), arsenic, cyanide, lead, benzene, carbon tetrachloride or carbolic acid, or any "remedy" taken by mouth that contains kerosene — those are poisons. The safe staples in the same books are soap, washing soda, borax, vinegar and absorbent powders.

🌾 Food From Scratch How to make staple ingredients — flour, masa, leavening, salt, sweetener, fat — from what grows or can be raised around the Illinois Valley, and how to turn them into bread, tortillas, pasta, crackers and other everyday food. Details and more recipes are in Food-From-Scratch\ (grain, wild and local staples, breads and staples) and Gardening-Food\. ⚠️ Two foods here can kill if you get them wrong: camas has a deadly look-alike (death camas), and acorns and lye/ash-cooked corn must be processed properly. Follow the steps exactly, and never eat a wild plant you can't identify with certainty.

🌾 Flour from grain - Grow hulless varieties of oats and barley if you can — hulled types need dehulling. Wheat and corn are the easiest staples to grow and grind. - Harvest when the heads are fully tan and nodding and the kernels are too hard to dent with a fingernail. Cut about 10 inches below the heads. - Thresh by stomping the heads in a clean bin or on a tarp; winnow by pouring the grain slowly in front of a fan (or in a breeze) so the chaff blows away. Repeat. (SARE handout) - Dry to 12–13% moisture before storing — wetter grain heats, molds and draws insects. Field test: a dry kernel resists your thumbnail and cracks sharply between your teeth. (Peace Corps Small Farm Grain Storage) - Store whole grain, grind as needed. Whole grain keeps for years; flour goes rancid within months once milled. A hand grain mill is worth owning; otherwise grind between two stones and sift out the bran. - Kill pests in stored grain: freeze small bags 2–3 days, or heat a ½-inch layer at 140–150 °F for 30 minutes (may weaken bread rise). Store airtight, and only when dry.

🌰 Acorn flour Our oaks — tanoak (the traditional favorite), California black oak, Oregon white oak and canyon live oak — all make good flour, but every acorn must be leached to remove bitter tannins. 1. Gather sound acorns in fall, dry them, crack and shell them, and remove any moldy or wormy ones. Grind the nutmeats to a coarse meal or flour. 2. Leach — any one of these: - Hot: soak in hot water for an hour, drain, repeat several times (fastest). - Running water: a cloth bag of meal in cold running water for several hours. - Daily change: 3 parts water to 1 part meal in jars, kept cool; pour off the dark water and refill every day for about a week. - Traditional: pour nearly scalding water over fine flour in a hollow scooped in clean sand. 3. It's done when it tastes sweet, not bitter or puckery. Cold leaching keeps more of the starch's binding power (better for bread); hot is faster. 4. Use it wet as mush/porridge, pat it into flatbread on a hot stone or pan, or dry it and replace ¼ to ½ of the wheat flour in bread (acorn flour has no gluten on its own).

🌿 Camas, cattail and other local starches - Camas bulbs (meadows, blue flowers in spring) were a major food here. They must be pit-roasted or slow-baked 24–36 hours — long cooking turns the indigestible starch sweet. Dry cooked bulbs or cakes for storage. ⚠️ Death camas grows in the same meadows and its bulbs look the same. Flower color is not a safe test. Only harvest from a bed you have watched bloom and learned plant by plant; if there's any doubt, leave it. (USDA Great Camas guide; Wild-Plants\ death camas guide) - Cattail: young shoots and stem bases (boiled or roasted), green flower spikes (boiled like corn), pollen to stretch flour, and rhizome flour (the root core is 30–46% starch — pound, soak, let the starch settle, dry it). Harvest only from clean water; cattails take up pollutants. - More: USDA Food Plants of the North American Indians lists about 1,100 native food plants and how each was prepared.

🌽 Corn: masa, tortillas and hominy Always cook dried corn with lime or wood ash ("nixtamal") before making it a staple — it unlocks the corn's niacin. People living mostly on untreated cornmeal get pellagra. - Masa with lime (food-grade slaked lime, cal): use lime 1% of the dry corn's weight (5 g of lime per 500 g of corn — weigh it if you can) and water 1½ times the corn's volume. Heat to just below a simmer (200–210 °F) until the skins slip off but the center is still firm (often under 30 minutes). Rest 8–12 hours in the liquid, then rub and rinse off the skins. Grind while cold; use the masa within a day. (Smithsonian method) - With wood ash instead: boil shelled corn 15–30 minutes in weak lye water made from hardwood ashes until the hulls loosen, then rinse very thoroughly in running water until no lye remains. Lye is caustic — gloves and eye protection; never taste it. - Corn tortillas: knead masa with a little water to a soft, play-dough feel, press balls flat between plastic or cloth, and cook on a hot dry griddle about a minute a side. - Hominy (whole kernels) and cornbread, mush, polenta and corn pone recipes: USDA Corn and Its Uses as Food (FB 1236).

🍞 Leavening without store yeast or baking powder - Wild sourdough starter: mix equal weights of flour (whole-grain or rye starts fastest) and unchlorinated water in a jar. Every day, discard all but a little and feed it equal weights of flour and water (twice a day from day 4). Keep it at 70–82 °F. Usable around day 7, strong in 2–4 weeks — it's ready when it doubles within 4–6 hours of feeding. Throw it out if mold appears. (Illinois Sourdough 101) - Keep it going: save ½ cup each time you bake; the night before, feed it equal parts flour and water and leave it warm 6–8 hours. Store in glass, not metal. - Back-up: spread some starter thin, dry it until brittle, and store it airtight. Revive by crumbling into warm water overnight, then feeding. - Potato yeast and "saving a piece of dough" for next time: USDA Bread and Bread Making (FB 807). - Quick breads: sour milk or buttermilk + ½ tsp baking soda per cup replaces sweet milk and baking powder. Homemade baking powder = 1 part baking soda : 2 parts cream of tartar.

🧂 Salt, 🍯 sweeteners and 🥓 fat - Salt from seawater: seawater is about 3.5% salt — roughly 4–5 gallons per pound of salt in practice. Collect it away from harbors and outfalls, filter through cloth, boil down to a slush, then finish drying slowly; pour off the last bitter liquid for better taste. - Bigleaf maple syrup (OSU 2025 guide): tap after leaf drop and a hard freeze, through winter freeze–thaw days, until buds break. 5/16-inch spile in a 2-inch hole; collect sap daily and boil it within 24 hours. Bigleaf sap is thin — about 80 gallons of sap per gallon of syrup (20 gallons ≈ 1 quart after ~8 hours of boiling). Syrup is done at 7 °F above the boiling point of water where you are — about 216 °F around Cave Junction's elevation (219 °F at sea level). - Honey: strain through progressively finer cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief). - Lard and tallow: chill fat and render it within about a week. Melt slowly with a little water, stirring, at 235–245 °F (no copper pots), until bubbling stops and the cracklings float and turn chestnut-brown; strain into clean jars, fill full, store cool and dark. - Nut oil (hazelnuts, acorns): grind, boil with water, and skim the oil as it rises; clarify and

turn chestnut-brown; strain into clean jars, fill full, store cool and dark. - Nut oil (hazelnuts, acorns): grind, boil with water, and skim the oil as it rises; clarify and store cool (Practical Action brief).

🥖 Staples Basic yeast bread — per loaf (USDA FB 807): 1 cup lukewarm liquid, about 3 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 1 Tbsp sugar or honey, up to 1 Tbsp fat, and yeast (or ½ cup active sourdough starter in place of yeast and part of the liquid). Knead until smooth and springy, let it double, shape, let it rise again, and bake at about 400 °F for 40–50 minutes, until it sounds hollow when tapped. Simple sourdough loaf: 1 cup active starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4–8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2–4 hours more, bake at about 425 °F for 35–45 minutes. Flour tortillas / flatbread: 2 cups flour, ¼ cup lard, 1 tsp salt, about ¾ cup warm water. Knead, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cook on a hot dry pan 30–60 seconds a side. Works with part acorn or barley flour. Biscuits (USDA FB 1136): 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp baking powder (or the soda and sour milk swap above), 2 Tbsp fat, ⅔–¾ cup liquid. Bake hot (about 450 °F) 12–15 minutes. Pasta / egg noodles: 2 cups flour, 1 egg + 2 yolks, ½ tsp salt, about ⅓ cup water (or the old way: one egg, a pinch of salt and enough flour for a very stiff

flour, 1 egg + 2 yolks, ½ tsp salt, about ⅓ cup water (or the old way: one egg, a pinch of salt and enough flour for a very stiff dough). Knead 8–10 minutes, rest 10–20, roll paper-thin, cut ⅛–¼ inch strips. Cook fresh 2–4 minutes, dried 10–12. To store, dry until the noodles snap; keep airtight about a month (longer frozen). (Illinois Extension; Fannie Farmer 1896) Hardtack (keeps for years): 3 parts flour to 1 part water (no salt — salt draws moisture and mold), stiff dough, ½ inch thick, prick with holes, bake 1 hour at 375 °F, then dry 3 more days. Soak or crumble into soup to eat. Beans: soak overnight (6 cups water + 2 tsp salt per pound) or quick-soak (boil 2 minutes, stand 1 hour), then simmer 2–4 hours. Old beans take longer; lentils and split peas need no soak. Beans + corn (or wheat) together make complete protein. Porridge and mush: cracked wheat, oats, barley, cornmeal or leached acorn meal simmered in about 3–4 times their volume of water with a pinch of salt.Old recipes in these books are fine for methods; for food safety (canning, curing, storing) follow the modern USDA guides in Gardening-Food\.

🐴 Horses, Mules and Draft Animals How to keep, feed, handle, ride, shoe and pack horses, mules and donkeys, and how to put them to work in harness — written for a time when there may be no feed store, vet or farrier. The manuals are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ (Care-Feeding, Riding-Training, Hoof-Care-Shoeing, Packing-Travel, Draft-Harness). Horse health, vital signs, colic and first aid are in Animals\ and the Animals and vet care section of the Illinois Valley page. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - A horse can kill you without meaning to. Stay where it can see you, speak before you touch it, keep a hand on it as you move around the hindquarters, and never stand directly behind or in front of it. - Never wrap a lead rope or reins around your hand or body, and never tie a horse with a knot you can't pull loose. Never tie with a chain lead. - Wear a helmet and boots with a heel when riding. - The old books here (1867–1940s) teach good handling and shoeing but also harsh "breaking" methods and dangerous old medicines (purges, firing, chloroform). Use them for skills, not for doctoring.

🐎 Choosing an animal - For a first horse, pick an older, calm, well-trained one (roughly 8–15 years) over a young or green horse. Check it sound before you take it: walk and trot it on hard ground, look for limping, swellings, bad feet and bad habits. (USDA How to Select a Sound Horse) - Age by the teeth: after about 12 years the front teeth turn triangular and slant forward. (USDA AIB 353) - Mules are tough, sure-footed, eat less and handle heat and rough country better; they tend to stand and fight rather than bolt. A well-trained mule is very steady; a badly trained one is hard work. Donkeys need shelter always — their coats aren't waterproof, which matters in our wet winters. (Donkey Care Handbook)

🌾 Feeding and water - Total feed: 1.5–2.5% of body weight a day, most of it hay or pasture. Never less than 8–10 lb of hay a day for a 1,000-lb horse; an idle horse holds weight on about 18 lb of good hay. (Nebraska G1781; FM 25-5) - Weigh a horse with a string: weight (lb) = heart girth (in) × heart girth (in) × body length (in) ÷ 330. Body length is point of shoulder to point of buttock. (G1781) - Working horses: about 1.1 lb grain + 1.25 lb hay per 100 lb of body weight a day, grain split into 3 feeds. Keep each grain meal under about 5 lb for a 1,000-lb horse. Feed by weight: a quart of oats ≈ 1 lb, a quart of corn ≈ 1.7 lb. (USDA FB1419; UGA B1356) - Water: 5–15 gallons a day, double in heat or hard work. Give an exhausted horse small drinks every 5–10 minutes until it recovers. In cold weather, take the chill off the water or salt the feed so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356; FM 25-5) - Salt: about 3 oz a day; loose salt-mineral beats a block. Western Oregon soils are low in selenium — use a mineral that contains it. (Rule of thumb) (AIB 353) - Army feeding rules that prevent colic: water before feeding (or wait

Oregon soils are low in selenium — use a mineral that contains it. (Rule of thumb) (AIB 353) - Army feeding rules that prevent colic: water before feeding (or wait an hour after); never grain a hot horse (hay is fine); a little hay before grain; change feeds gradually over 1–2 weeks; never feed moldy or dusty hay. (FM 25-5) - Body condition: keep them at 5–7 on the 1–9 scale — feel ribs, back and tailhead with your hands; a winter coat hides thinness. (G1781)

🦷 Teeth and worms - Teeth: check at least yearly. Sharp edges form on the outside of the upper molars and inside of the lowers — float (rasp) them or the horse drops feed and loses weight. (PNW 587; Merillat Animal Dentistry) - Worms: don't deworm blindly every 8 weeks. Adults need 1–2 treatments a year (one in fall for bots and tapeworms); youngsters 3–4. When dewormers run out: pick up manure, don't overgraze, rotate pastures and graze with cattle or sheep. (Penn State/SARE)

🦶 Hoof care and shoeing - Pick out the feet every day. A healthy frog feels like firm rubber. Thrush (black, stinking rot in the frog) comes from wet, dirty footing — trim away dead tissue, apply an antiseptic, and get the horse onto dry ground. In our wet winters, give horses a dry gravel or wood-chip standing area. (TM 2-220; PNW 587; OSU EC1558) - Hooves grow about ⅜ inch a month. Trim barefoot horses every 6–12 weeks, donkeys and mules every 6–10; the Army reset shoes every 3–6 weeks. (NMSU B-707; TM 2-220) - Going barefoot (when shoes and nails run out): leave the sole, balance the wall, round off the outer edge so it doesn't chip, and check weekly. Most horses do fine barefoot on soft ground; hard rocky work wears feet faster than they grow. (TM 2-220) - Making and fitting shoes: TM 2-220 The Horseshoer teaches forging shoes from bar stock, fitting and nailing, and even shoeing in the field with a ground fire and a rail for an anvil. Lungwitz's Text-Book of Horseshoeing is the standard reference. Pair with the Blacksmithing guide.

🤠 Handling, saddling and riding - Leading: from the left side, right hand near the halter, slack folded (never wrapped) in your left hand. (PNW 587) - Tying: use a quick-release knot, about 3 ft of rope, tied at or above withers height to something solid. Any rope around the neck gets a bowline (it can't tighten), never a slip knot. Untie before taking the halter off. (PNW 587) - Saddle fit: with pad and rider on, the gullet must clear the withers. After a sweaty ride, even sweat marks = good fit; dry spots = pressure. A sliding saddle needs a breast collar, not a tighter cinch. (UF Saddle Fit) - Cinching: snug it gradually until a flat hand just slips under, walk the horse a few steps, then recheck after a short ride — many horses puff up their bellies. On the trail, stop after 1–2 miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse, sit deep with heels down. The 4-H manual (PNW 587) and FM 25-5 walk through riding step by step. - Starting young horses: handle foals early and teach them to lead before weaning. Light harness or saddle work at 2–3 years; no heavy work until they're nearly mature. First tie with a neck rope through the halter ring, tied with

lead before weaning. Light harness or saddle work at 2–3 years; no heavy work until they're nearly mature. First tie with a neck rope through the halter ring, tied with a bowline. (USDA FB1368) - Tack repair: cutting leather, hand-stitching with waxed thread and riveting are in TM 10-430 The Saddler and Hasluck's Harness Making.

🎒 Travel and packing | | | | Walk / trot | about 4 mph / 8–9 mph | | Steady day's travel | 20+ miles on easy ground, 10–15 in mountains | | Rider | no more than about 20% of the horse's weight (250 lb max) | | Pack load | 200–250 lb per 900–1,000-lb animal; 300 lb only short-distance | | Load balance | side packs within 2–3 lb of each other | (FM 25-5; FM 25-7; USFS Instructions on Horse Packing; Montana outfitters manual) - On the road: rest 5–10 minutes every hour; every 2–3 hours unsaddle, let the horse roll and graze. Walk them up steep hills. Only hardened horses can do 40–50 miles a day for days on end. Condition animals 2–4 weeks before hard travel. (Animal Management) - Packing: sawbuck and Decker pack saddles, hitches and loading are in the 1943 Forest Service manual (written for Oregon and Washington) and FM 25-7, which also shows improvised pack saddles and a travois.

🚜 Harness and draft work - What an animal can pull all day: about one-tenth of its body weight in steady draft (a big horse pulling 150 lb at 2½ mph ≈ 1 horsepower). Donkeys pull about a fifth of their weight for 3–4 hours. A cart donkey should pull no more than twice its weight, cart included, on the flat. (Peace Corps Animal Traction; Donkey Care Handbook) - Collar fit: a flat hand should just pass between the collar and the windpipe. A short collar chokes; a long one bruises the shoulders. Give each horse its own collar and wipe it after every use. Sore shoulders are the #1 harness problem. (USDA FB1419; FM 25-5) - Harness, hitching, driving pairs and teams, carts, plows and sledges: FM 25-5, Mounted Instruction for Field Artillery, the Peace Corps Animal Traction manual and Starkey's Harnessing and Implements. Big-team hitches and eveners: Sommerfeld's How to Hitch Horses.

☠️ Local dangers - Toxic plants: tansy ragwort, poison and water hemlock, foxglove and bracken fern — hungry horses on overgrazed pasture eat them. (Wild-Plants\ and Animals\ sheets) - Wildfire: evacuate horses early and in daylight; practice loading into a trailer ahead of time. See the Illinois Valley page.Old military feeding rules assume plenty of oats and hay; scale rations to what you can grow, and watch body condition.

⛽ Fuel Guide How long gasoline, diesel, kerosene and propane keep, how to tell when fuel has gone bad, what can be rescued, how to store fuel for the long haul — and how to get fuel out of gas-station underground tanks, drums and vehicles when there's no grid power. The manuals are in Fuel\ (Fuel-Quality-Storage, Station-Tanks-Pumping, Military-Fuel-Handling, Other-Fuels). Wood gas, biodiesel and alcohol fuel are in Homestead-Skills\Fuels. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent fires and deaths - Gasoline vapor explodes. No flames, smoking or sparks within 50 feet of open fuel. Use only pumps made for gasoline — ordinary electric motors spark. - Static sparks ignite fuel. Touch bare metal with your bare hand before opening any cap. Keep the nozzle touching the can or tank the whole time you pour. Fill portable cans on the ground, never in a truck bed or on carpet. (FM 10-67-1) - Never climb into a tank sump, manway or tank. Fuel vapor pushes out oxygen and can kill without any smell or warning; the lids are heavy. Work from ground level. (EPA; DoD UFM) - Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater or lamp, and never store fuel inside the house. - Propane sinks into basements and ditches. Smell gas: put out flames, get out, close the tank valve if it's safe. (Texas RRC)

🕰️ How long fuel keeps | Fuel | Keeps (cool, sealed, full container) | Notes | | Gasoline with ethanol (E10) | about 2–3 months | Most pump gas. Absorbs water, then separates. (K-State MF3068; Oklahoma BAE-1746) | | Ethanol-free gasoline | about 6 months or more | Kept nearly full and cool. (Alberta Farm Fuel Storage) | | Gasoline + stabilizer added when fresh | about 1–2 years (rule of thumb) | Stabilizer slows aging; it can't fix fuel that's already stale. | | Diesel | 6–12 months, years with care | Keep water out, use a biocide, test and filter. (Chevron; Alberta) | | Kerosene (1-K) | longer than gasoline (rule of thumb) | Keep in blue cans, sealed. | | Propane | doesn't go bad (rule of thumb) | The tank and valve are what wear out. | Storage that makes fuel last: fill containers nearly full (less air), keep them cool and out of the sun, use metal or approved cans with tight caps, add stabilizer the day you buy the fuel, label the date, and use the oldest first. Keep fuel outside living areas.

🔍 Is this fuel still good? - Jar test: pour a sample from the bottom of the can or tank into a clean clear jar. Good fuel is clear and bright. Let it stand 15 minutes. Haze, droplets or a second layer at the bottom = water. Water fully settles out in about a day. (FM 10-67-2) - Bad signs: darker color, a sour or varnish smell, or a drop on glass that leaves a sticky film when it dries (gum). Gum sticks valves and clogs carburetors. - E10 with a bottom layer has phase-separated: the bottom is ethanol plus water, not just water. E10 at 60 °F holds only about 4 teaspoons of water per gallon before this happens — less in the cold. Humid air rarely causes it; rain and water sitting in tanks do. (EPA phase-separation memo)

🔧 Rescuing old fuel (FM 10-67-2 Petroleum Testing) - Water and dirt can be fixed: let the fuel settle a few hours to a day, then pour or siphon off the top, leaving the bottom inch behind, and filter it. - Phase-separated E10: the layers won't remix. Drain off and discard the bottom layer. The top is weaker (lower-octane) gasoline — fine for lawn, farm and older carbureted engines. - Stale but clean gasoline: blend it with fresh. The Army mixes a small test batch first. Rule of thumb: 1 part old to 4 or more parts fresh for mildly stale gas, and use it in simple engines (generators, mowers, older trucks) — not modern high-compression or turbo engines. The staler it is, the more fresh fuel it needs. - Can't be fixed: heavy gum and varnish, and gasoline mixed into diesel — even 1% gasoline makes diesel much more flammable to handle. (Chevron Diesel Fuels Review) - Starting on old gas: a little fresh gas or starting fluid in the carburetor helps it catch; stale gas has lost the light parts that make it start. (Rule of thumb)

🛢️ Diesel care - Water is the enemy. Drain water from the bottom of tanks and drums regularly, and check for it every time you gauge. Keep drum bungs tight and covered so rain can't seep in. (FM 10-67-1) - "Diesel bug": yeast, fungus and bacteria grow where fuel meets water — brown or black slime that clogs filters. Prevent with zero water and a biocide; badly slimed tanks must be drained and scrubbed. Expect old station diesel tanks to be corroded inside. (DoD UFM; EPA) - Cold gelling: thin diesel with No. 1 diesel or kerosene (the Army blends kerosene in for winter) or add a cold-flow additive — before it gets cold; additives won't un-gel it. - Substitutes: diesel engines can run on No. 2 heating oil; kerosene and Jet A are close to No. 1 diesel. Kerosene is "dry" (low lubricity) and harder on modern injection pumps; older mechanical-pump diesels tolerate substitutes best. (Rule of thumb) (FEMA P-1019)

🏪 Getting fuel out of gas-station tanks What's under the concrete (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets; North Dakota training): - Each tank is usually 8,000–20,000 gallons, about 8–10 ft across, with its bottom roughly 10–14 ft below the pavement. (Rule of thumb) - Fill pipes sit inside small round spill buckets (lids 1–2 ft). The cap colors usually tell you the fuel: white = regular, blue = mid-grade, red = premium, yellow = diesel; orange marks vapor-recovery pipes, not fuel. (Rule of thumb — check by gauging.) - A large manhole (3–4 ft lid) right over each tank covers the turbine-pump sump — the pump, piping and leak sensor. Other small risers are the tank gauge, spare ports and vents. Step 1 — measure what's there (EPA Doing Inventory Control Right): - Use a long wooden stick (won't spark) marked in inches. Lower it straight down the fill pipe until it touches bottom, hold it 5–10 seconds for gasoline, and read the wet line. - Water-finding paste on the tip changes color where there's water in the bottom. A tank chart (if you can find one in the station office) converts inches to gallons. Step 2 — the easy way: power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser — power the dispenser and it pumps. - At most modern stations the pump is the submersible

power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser — power the dispenser and it pumps. - At most modern stations the pump is the submersible turbine in the sump, usually 240-volt, ¾–2 hp, plus the dispenser's electronics. That takes a stout generator. Connect only through the station's transfer switch (many stations in hurricane states are prewired for one) — never by backfeeding. (Florida SB 528 analysis; NASEO) If the owner is around, work with them: they know their tanks and may already have a generator hookup. Step 3 — no power: pump it up by hand. - A siphon won't work — the fuel is below you, and a siphon only flows downhill. - Hose down the fill pipe: there's a drop tube inside with a flapper valve (it slams shut near full) that ends about 6 inches above the tank bottom. A smooth hose usually slides past when the tank isn't full, but it can snag; the separate gauge port is another way in. (Vermont Simple Suction manual; EPA) - Suction lift is the limit. Hand and 12-volt suction pumps typically lift gasoline 10 feet or less (less in hot weather — gasoline boils in the hose). They work while the tank is fairly full and fail as it drops. (Rule of thumb, from the physics in FM 10-67-1) - For a deep or

in the hose). They work while the tank is fairly full and fail as it drops. (Rule of thumb, from the physics in FM 10-67-1) - For a deep or low tank, use a pump that goes down into the tank — a 12-volt submersible fuel-transfer pump rated for gasoline on a long hose — or a hand pump on a long rigid pipe. - Keep the hose end a few inches off the bottom to avoid water and sludge, pump into metal cans on the ground, keep everything bonded (metal-to-metal contact or a ground wire), and filter through a water-separating funnel.

🚗 Drums and vehicles - Drums: a rotary or lever drum hand pump threads into the 2-inch bung; the Army's have a bonding wire and a strainer. Keep the drum grounded. (FM 10-67-1) - Cars and trucks: most modern fillers have an anti-siphon screen or rollover valve, so a hose won't reach the fuel. It's usually easier to disconnect the fuel line at the engine and let the car's own fuel pump push fuel into a can (key on, or power the pump relay) — or drain from the fuel-filter or tank fittings underneath. Older vehicles and many diesel trucks have no screen. (Rule of thumb) - Gas in old vehicles goes stale too — jar-test it before trusting it.

🔥 Kerosene and propane - Kerosene heaters: only water-clear 1-K kerosene, never gasoline (even a little is dangerous). Store it in blue cans that have never held gasoline. Refuel outdoors with the heater off and cool; crack a window — unvented heaters make carbon monoxide. (CPSC) - Propane: store cylinders outdoors and upright, never in a closed building; vapor is heavier than air and pools low. After a flood, have tanks and lines checked before use. (Texas RRC)Fuel numbers vary with temperature, blend and storage. When in doubt, test a small batch in a simple engine before trusting old fuel in anything important.

⚒️ Blacksmithing and Hand Tools How to set up a simple forge, pick the right scrap steel, forge and heat-treat it, and make or repair basic hand tools — chisels, punches, tongs, knives, axes — plus how to sharpen and re-handle the tools you already have. The full books are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ (Blacksmithing, Heat-Treating-Steel, Hand-Tools); axe and crosscut-saw manuals are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst injuries - Hot steel looks exactly like cold steel. Assume everything near the forge is hot; pick things up with tongs, and set hot pieces down where no one will grab them. - Eye protection at the anvil, grinder and when quenching. Never use a cracked grinding wheel, never wear gloves at the wheel, stand aside when you switch it on. (Navy Steelworker) - Never heat galvanized (zinc-coated) metal indoors — the fumes cause "metal fume fever." Strip the zinc first (rule of thumb: soak overnight in vinegar) and work outdoors. Drinking milk does not help, despite old advice. (TM 10-440) - Quench oil can catch fire. Use a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an oil fire — smother it with the lid. (Rule of thumb) - A coal or charcoal forge makes carbon monoxide — work outdoors
and completely. Never put water on an oil fire — smother it with the lid. (Rule of thumb) - A coal or charcoal forge makes carbon monoxide — work outdoors or under an open-sided roof.

🔥 A simple forge and anvil Rule-of-thumb setups; the books have full plans. - Forge: anything that holds a fist-sized pile of burning fuel with air blown up into the middle — a brake drum or steel tub lined with clay, or a brick or stone hearth with a pipe coming in at the bottom (the "tuyere"). The ICS Shop Equipment book and the Peace Corps manual show how to build forges and bellows. - Air: a hand-crank blower, homemade bellows, a hair dryer or a small fan with a valve or gate to control it. Too much air wastes fuel and burns steel. - Fuel: charcoal (easy to make — see Homestead-Skills\Fuels), or coal turned to coke in the fire. Keep the fire clean: rake out clinker (glassy lumps), and work in the hot center. - Anvil: a real anvil is best, but a chunk of railroad rail, a big block of steel, or a sledgehammer head set in a stump works. Set the face at about knuckle height when you stand with your arm hanging. - First tools: a 2–3 lb cross-peen hammer, a pair of tongs (or make them — they're a classic first project), a bucket of water, a file, and a magnet.

🌡️ Heat colors (in shade, not sunlight) | Color | What it's for | | Dull red | Stop hammering — steel worked colder than this cracks. | | Cherry red | Hardening temperature for most carbon steel; bending. | | Orange to yellow | Normal forging heat — hammer here. | | Bright yellow-white, "flowing" surface | Forge welding (mild steel and wrought iron, about 2,000 °F). | | White with sparks shooting off | Burned. The steel is ruined — cut that part off. | High-carbon steel burns at a lower heat than mild steel, so forge tool steel no hotter than orange-yellow. (TM 10-440) Basic moves: drawing out (hammering thinner and longer), upsetting (hammering the hot end to make it thicker), bending over the anvil horn or edge, punching holes hot, cutting on a hardy (a chisel set in the anvil), twisting, and forge welding. Ilgen's Forge Work and the Selvidge Shop Manual walk through each one step by step.

🔩 Which scrap steel to use (Peace Corps Basic Techniques of Blacksmithing) | Steel | Found in | Good for | | Low carbon — won't harden | Car body panels, most rebar, nails, bolts, rail spikes, pipe, drums | Hooks, hinges, brackets, tongs, anything that bends instead of cuts. Forge-welds easily. | | Medium carbon — hardens | Leaf and coil springs, axles, torsion bars, shock-absorber rods | Chisels, punches, hammers, axes, hoes, pry bars, springs. The best all-round tool stock. | | High carbon — hardens hard | Old files, saw blades, drill bits, dies, bulldozer blades | Knives, scrapers, wood chisels, plane irons — tools that must hold a keen edge. | - Quick test: heat the tip to light cherry red and quench it in water. If a file skates over it like glass, it will harden. If the file bites, it's low-carbon. - Spark test on a grinder: low-carbon steel throws long streams with few forks; high-carbon throws shorter, bushier streams full of bright bursts; cast iron throws short dull red sparks. Practice on known pieces first. (Navy Steelworker)

🧪 Hardening and tempering 1. Anneal (soften) old steel before reshaping it cold or filing it: heat slowly to red, then bury it in dry wood ashes, lime or powdered charcoal and leave it until cold. (Selvidge) 2. Harden: heat evenly to cherry red — rule of thumb: just past the point where a magnet stops sticking to it — and quench. - Plain carbon steel (springs, files, most scrap): water or brine (about ¾ lb salt per gallon) cools fastest and most evenly. Thin or very high-carbon pieces (files, knives) can crack in water — warm oil (80–150 °F; vegetable oil works) is gentler. - Alloy steels: oil only. - The steel is now glass-hard and brittle — temper it right away, before it's fully cold. (Navy Steelworker) 3. Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven) and watch the colors run. Quench when the edge reaches the color you want: | Color | About | Use | | Pale yellow | 430 °F | Engraving and lathe tools, scrapers | | Straw | 460 °F | Taps, punches, dies, knives for a very hard edge | | Brown-yellow (deep straw) | 500 °F | Wood chisels, drills, plane irons, hammer faces | | Purple | 530–540 °F | Light cold chisels, shears,

very hard edge | | Brown-yellow (deep straw) | 500 °F | Wood chisels, drills, plane irons, hammer faces | | Purple | 530–540 °F | Light cold chisels, shears, axes | | Blue tinged with purple | 550 °F | Ordinary cold chisels | | Blue | 570–600 °F | Springs, picks | The further toward blue, the softer and tougher. Books disagree a little — one old table puts most chisels and knives at light blue — so test your tool and adjust. (Selvidge; Bacon; TM 10-440) One-heat method for chisels and punches: heat the working end to cherry red, quench only the tip inch or so (bob it up and down), pull it out, quickly polish the tip, and watch the heat from the shank run colors toward the edge. When the right color reaches the edge, quench the whole tool. (Selvidge; Steelworker)

🛠️ Making basic tools - Cold chisel (first real project): a 6–8 inch piece of coil spring or axle. Straighten it, draw one end to a wedge, grind or file the edge to about 60°, harden and temper to purple at the edge (one-heat method). Leave the striking end soft. - Center punch / drift: same steel, drawn to a round taper; temper the point straw to brown. - Tongs: two matching pieces of mild steel, forged with jaws and a boss, punched and riveted together. Richardson Vol 2 and Selvidge have patterns. - Knife: from an old file or saw blade. Anneal first, forge or grind to shape (on a grinder, dip often — blue on the edge means you've ruined the temper), harden in oil, temper straw to brown. - Axe, hoe, hammer: the Peace Corps manual covers forging each from scrap, including punching the eye with a drift. - Repairing tools ("dressing"): reforge mushroomed chisel heads, re-point picks, and redraw worn hoes and drill bits — ICS Shop Equipment, Hand Forging and Tool Dressing.

🪓 Keeping hand tools working Hanging an axe handle (USFS An Ax to Grind): - Line the edge up with the center of the handle. Laid flat, the blade should touch the table one third of the way from the heel. - Saw the wedge slot about two-thirds of the depth of the eye. Drive the head on by striking the end of the handle on a block, not the head. - Drive a hardwood wedge in until it stops, leaving ¼–½ inch, then trim. No metal wedges, screws or epoxy. Soaking a loose head in water only works for a day. - Good handle woods: straight-grained ash (Oregon ash grows here), hickory, oak. (Rule of thumb) Sharpening: - Never sharpen an axe on a fast dry bench grinder — it draws the temper (the edge turns blue). Use a file (cuts on the push stroke only; lift on the return, wear gloves and use a knuckle guard), a slow wet grindstone, then a whetstone. File until a burr forms, then switch sides. Aim for about 25°, slightly convex. (An Ax to Grind; Handtools for Trail Work) - Chisels and plane irons: grind at about 25°, then hone on an oilstone or water stone until a fine burr forms, flip and flatten the back, and strop. (Griffith Essentials of Woodworking) - Hand saws (Disston): clamp with the gullets just above

oilstone or water stone until a fine burr forms, flip and flatten the back, and strop. (Griffith Essentials of Woodworking) - Hand saws (Disston): clamp with the gullets just above the jaws. Joint the teeth level with a flat file, set them (never deeper than half the tooth), then file. Crosscut: every other tooth with the file angled about 45° toward the handle, then turn the saw around for the rest. Rip: straight across at 90°. - Files: keep them dry and separate (files dull each other), clean them with a file card or a nail, and use chalk on the teeth for soft metals. (Nicholson Treatise on Files and Rasps)The old books use coal forges and some chemicals now known to be dangerous (cyanide for case-hardening, asbestos). Use their methods, not their chemicals.

🍄 Mushroom Guide How to identify, use, preserve and grow mushrooms in the Illinois Valley — and how not to die doing it. The field guides, poisoning reports and growing manuals are in Mushrooms\ (Identification, Poisoning-Safety, Uses-Growing-Preserving). Wild-Plants\ also has the Forest Service Wild Edible Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest and death cap ID sheets. ### ⚠️ The rules that keep foragers alive 1. Only eat a mushroom you have identified with complete certainty — every feature, including the spore print and the base of the stem. "Pretty sure" is how people die. 2. No folk test works. Silver turning dark, a peeling cap, animals or insects eating it, soaking in salt water, cooking — none of these tell you anything. Cooking, drying, freezing and canning do not destroy the deadly toxins. (FDA Bad Bug Book) 3. The deadliest ones taste fine and make you sick late — 6 to 24 hours or more after eating. By then the toxin is already in your liver or kidneys. 4. Dig up the whole mushroom — the cup or bulb at the base is what tells you it's a deadly Amanita. Never eat unopened "buttons" of gilled mushrooms; nobody can tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in moderation, and keep one uncooked

deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in moderation, and keep one uncooked specimen in the fridge in case someone gets sick.

🔎 How to identify a mushroom Check all of these, every time: - Underside: gills (thin blades), pores (a sponge of tubes — boletes), teeth or spines (hedgehogs), or blunt ridges (chanterelles). - Stem base: dig it up. A cup (volva) or bulb at the base, plus a ring on the stem and white gills, means Amanita — leave all of them alone. (FB 796) - Spore print: cut off the stem of a mature cap, lay the cap gills-down on half white, half dark paper, cover with a glass, and wait a few hours. The color (white, pink, brown, rusty, purple-black) places the mushroom in its family. (Thomas Field Book; Atkinson) - Where it grows: on wood or soil, under which trees (oak, tanoak, Douglas-fir, pine), alone or in clumps, and the season. - Flesh, smell and bruising: does it stain when cut? Is the flesh brittle or stringy?

☠️ The killers that grow around here | Mushroom | What it looks like | What it does | | Death cap (Amanita phalloides) | Greenish-olive to yellowish or white cap, white gills, white ring, bulb in a cup at the base. Under oaks and filberts (hazelnuts), wet season. | Liver failure. One cap can kill an adult. Poisoned 5 Oregonians in 1988; 4 needed liver transplants. | | Western destroying angel (Amanita ocreata) | All-white, cup at the base, under oaks. Oregon cases on record. | Liver and kidney failure. | | Deadly Galerina (Galerina marginata) | Small, brown, on rotting wood, rusty-brown spore print, often a thin ring. Easily mistaken for "little brown" edibles. | Same toxin as death cap. | | Deadly parasols (small Lepiota) | Small, scaly-capped, white gills, on soil. | Same toxin as death cap. | | Amanita smithiana | White, shaggy; grows right next to matsutake in our tanoak forests. Brittle flesh. | Kidney failure. | | Deadly webcaps (Cortinarius, orellanine) | Orange to red-brown, dry, fibrous cap, rusty gills, under conifers. | Kidney failure, 3–14 days later. | | False morels (Gyromitra) | Brain-like or saddle-shaped cap, not pitted, chambered stem. | Vomiting, seizures, liver damage; fumes from cooking can poison the cook. | (CDC 2017 death-cap report; NAMA poisoning registry; PNW/BC White Paper; USFS reports) Poisoning timeline — deadly Amanita, Galerina,

Vomiting, seizures, liver damage; fumes from cooking can poison the cook. | (CDC 2017 death-cap report; NAMA poisoning registry; PNW/BC White Paper; USFS reports) Poisoning timeline — deadly Amanita, Galerina, Lepiota: nothing for 6–24 hours, then violent vomiting and diarrhea, then a false recovery around day 1–2, then liver (and kidney) failure at day 3–5. 10–20% die even with hospital care. (CDC MMWR 2017)

🚑 If someone may have eaten a bad mushroom - Get medical help immediately, even if they feel fine — the dangerous ones are delayed. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222. - Bring the mushroom — leftovers, the uncooked ones, even scraps from the trash — in a paper bag (they rot in plastic). A photo is far less useful than a sample. (White Paper) - Doctors treat amatoxin with IV fluids, repeated activated charcoal and liver-protecting drugs (NAMA treatment report). With no hospital: replace fluids constantly (oral rehydration solution — see the Medical guides), give activated charcoal if you have it, and rest. Survival odds are much worse without a hospital — which is why rule 1 matters so much.

🫙 Cooking, drying and storing - Cook all wild mushrooms — never raw, and morels especially well done. Don't mix alcohol with morels the first time (some people react). - Dry slices about ½ inch thick at about 120 °F with good airflow until crisp; morels lose about 90% of their weight. Store airtight. Rehydrate in hot water. Ventilate while drying — spores can trigger asthma. (OSU SP 50-919; USFS PNW-GTR-710) - Freeze after sautéing (best) or steam-blanching. - Never can wild mushrooms — only store-type button mushrooms have tested canning times.

🪵 Growing your own - Shiitake on logs: fresh hardwood logs (oak is among the best) 4–6 inches across, cut in the dormant season while the bark is tight. Drill holes 7/16 inch wide, 1¼ inches deep, 3 inches apart in a diamond pattern, plug with spawn, seal with wax. Keep shaded and moist. Mushrooms start in 6–18 months; after that, soak a log 24 hours and it fruits about a week later. Rest logs 8–12 weeks between soaks. (UVM/Cornell; USDA Agroforestry Note 13) - Oysters on straw: chop straw 4–5 inches, soak overnight, pasteurize at 165 °F for 1–2 hours, mix in 5–10% spawn, pack into bags with holes, keep warm and humid. Fruits in weeks. (UF IFAS SS662) - Keep your strain going: a piece of a fruiting log or colonized straw can start the next batch, so you don't need to buy spawn again.

🌿 Medicinal mushrooms Turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake have real research behind them as add-ons to treatment — turkey-tail extract (PSK) is a prescribed cancer add-on in Japan — but most evidence is from lab and animal studies. They are not cures. Turkey tail and reishi are traditionally simmered for hours as tea. (VA Mycomedicinals)The old mushroom books here (1895–1928) are great for pictures, descriptions and recipes, but some of their safety advice is wrong and has killed people: Marshall's Mushroom Book lists false morels as edible, Thomas says the parasol has no poisonous look-alike, and USDA FB 796 recommends raw mushrooms and old first aid. They also miss most western killers. Use the modern files in Poisoning-Safety and this guide for anything about safety.

☢️ Nuclear Fallout Guide What to do if there is a nuclear detonation or a radiation release: how to shelter, how long, how to protect food, water and animals, how to clean up, and when potassium iodide (KI) helps. The full manuals — shelter plans, the homemade KFM fallout meter, farm and livestock guides — are in Nuclear-Radiation\. ### The three rules 1. Get inside. Stay inside. Stay tuned. Most deaths from fallout are avoidable just by being behind enough mass in the first day or two. 2. Fallout is dust. It hurts you from what lands on and near you, so put mass and distance between you and the roof, walls and ground outside. 3. Time is on your side. Radiation from fallout drops fast — 90% in the first 7 hours, 99% in 2 days.

⚡ The first minutes - If you see a flash: drop behind anything solid, face down, cover your head, and don't look at it. The blast wave can arrive many seconds later — stay down until it passes. - Fallout near a blast can start arriving in 15–30 minutes; 100–200 miles downwind, often 5–10 hours or more. Use the time before it arrives to put out small fires, bring people, pets and water inside, and move to the best shelter you can reach. (FEMA Protection in the Nuclear Age, H-20) - Officials will tell everyone within about 50 miles to shelter until they know where the fallout is going. (FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed.)

🏠 Where to shelter Best to worst: a basement (especially a corner below ground level) → the middle floors and center of a large concrete or brick building → a crawl space or interior room of a house → a vehicle (poor). Most homes in the Illinois Valley are one-story wood frame with no basement. FEMA says these, and vehicles, are not adequate shelter on their own. Plan now: a nearby building with a basement or thick masonry, a crawl-space shelter you can shield, or an outdoor trench shelter (plans in MP-79, In Time of Emergency, and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix A). - Inside any building: get as far from the roof and outside walls as you can, away from windows and doors. Close and lock windows, turn off fans, A/C and forced-air heat, close fireplace dampers. (CDC Where to Go) - Stuck in a poor shelter? If a good one is under 15 minutes away, move within about 30 minutes of the blast, before heavy fallout arrives. If you're already in a moderate shelter, stay 1–2 hours, then move. (FEMA Planning Guidance) Adding shielding — each of these stops about as much as 4 inches of concrete (FEMA H-20): | Material | Thickness | | Brick | 5–6 in | | Sand or gravel | 6 in | | Packed earth | 7 in | | Hollow concrete

H-20): | Material | Thickness | | Brick | 5–6 in | | Sand or gravel | 6 in | | Packed earth | 7 in | | Hollow concrete block (sand-filled) | 8 in (6 in) | | Water | 10 in | | Books or magazines | 14 in | | Wood (firewood stack) | 18 in | Pile it on the floor above you and around the walls of your shelter spot: earth-filled drawers and boxes, water jugs, firewood, books, heavy furniture. Every extra ~4 inches of packed earth roughly halves what gets through — about 3 feet of earth cuts it around 1,000×. Crawl space: shelter under the center of the house, ring yourself with blocks or earth-filled containers, and pile mass on the floor above. Ventilation: a crowded, sealed shelter gets dangerously hot in warm weather. Kearny's homemade air pump (KAP) — plans in Nuclear War Survival Skills and the ORNL Expedient Shelter Handbook — moves air without bringing in fallout dust.

⏳ How long to stay in The 7-10 rule: every 7× increase in time after the blast cuts the radiation 10× (once the fallout has finished falling). | Time after blast | Radiation level (example) | | 1 hour | 1,000 R/hr | | 7 hours | 100 R/hr | | 2 days | 10 R/hr | | 2 weeks | 1 R/hr | - Stay sheltered at least 12–24 hours (FEMA). In heavy fallout areas it can be several days to two weeks, with only short trips out once levels drop (H-20). - Without a meter, listen for official word. With a meter, you can make your own decisions — see below.

🧼 Cleaning yourself up (decontamination) (CDC; EPA Protective Action Q&A) - Taking off your outer layer of clothes removes up to 90% of the fallout on you. Do it before you enter the shelter if you can. Bag the clothes and put them away from people and pets. - Shower with soap and shampoo — no conditioner (it glues particles to hair). Don't scrub hard or scratch the skin; keep cuts covered. - No shower? Wipe exposed skin, blow your nose, wipe eyelids, ears and face with a damp cloth. - Clothes from closed drawers and closets are fine to wear. - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing gloves and a dust mask, rinse completely, then wash yourself. - Fallout looks like sand, ash or grit. Brush or hose it off roofs and away from the house after levels drop; wear a dust mask, gloves and a hat, and wash afterward.

💊 Potassium iodide (KI) - KI only protects the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine. It does nothing against other fallout. Take it only when health officials say to — or, with no officials, when you have reason to believe fresh fallout or a reactor plume is arriving. Table salt and iodine tincture are not substitutes (tincture is poisonous to swallow). (CDC; FDA) - One dose protects about 24 hours. It works best just before or as the plume arrives and still helps 3–4 hours after. Avoid repeat doses for newborns and pregnant or breastfeeding women. (FDA) FDA dose by age (one dose per day): | Who | Dose | | Adults over 18 (including pregnant or breastfeeding) | 130 mg | | Ages 12–18 (130 mg if 154 lb or more) | 65 mg | | Ages 3–12 | 65 mg | | 1 month – 3 years | 32 mg | | Birth – 1 month | 16 mg | Adults over 40 need it only for a very large expected exposure. To make liquid doses for small children from tablets, use the two FDA sheets in Nuclear-Radiation\Government-Guidance.

🥫 Food and water (EPA Protective Action Q&A; FDA; Nuclear War Survival Skills Ch. 8) - Food that was indoors is fine. Sealed cans, jars and bags that were outside are fine after wiping the outside. Stored grain and canned food have no radioactive-iodine risk. - Don't eat garden produce or anything left uncovered outdoors until levels have dropped and it's declared clear — then wash and peel it. - Don't drink fresh milk from animals grazing fallout-covered pasture for the first weeks (radioactive iodine concentrates in milk). Milk made into cheese and aged two months or more is fine — the radioactive iodine decays away. - Water: bottled and sealed water is certain. Covered wells, tanks and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay soil, let it settle several hours, and pour off the clear water — or filter it through a bucket of packed earth. Both remove most fallout particles. Then disinfect as usual. - Cover rain barrels, tanks and well heads ahead of time.

🐄 Livestock and gardens (USDA FB 2107, PA-516; Oregon ODOE) - Shelter animals if you can (a barn helps), and take them off pasture. Feed protected feed — hay from inside the stack, covered silage, grain from closed bins. - Water from a covered well, tank or flowing spring is best; open pond water clears more slowly but improves quickly. - Hold off on slaughter, fresh milk and eggs until levels drop. - Gardens: stop harvesting; after levels drop, wash and peel produce. Fallout on soil decays and is diluted by digging it in.

📟 Measuring radiation - A meter turns guessing into decisions — when to leave the shelter, which room is safest, whether the water is clear. - KFM (Kearny Fallout Meter): a homemade meter from a can, foil and paper. Build it before you need it. The patterns must print exactly to scale — check against a ruler; OISM warns online copies of the templates aren't fully reliable and recommends the printed book. Full patterns and tables: ORNL-5040 and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix C. - Old civil-defense meters turn up at sales: the yellow CD V-715 reads high levels (fallout); the CD V-700 is a low-range Geiger counter for checking food, water and people. Manuals and a home-study course are in Nuclear-Radiation\Measuring-Radiation.

📍 Our area - The region's only operating nuclear power plant is the Columbia Generating Station at Hanford, Washington — roughly 350 miles from the Illinois Valley, far outside its planning zones. (Oregon ODOE) - The more realistic threats here are fallout drifting from detonations elsewhere and fallout carried across the Pacific on west winds. After Chernobyl, radioactive iodine showed up in milk in northwest Oregon. (Nuclear War Survival Skills) - OISM, publisher of Nuclear War Survival Skills, is in Cave Junction — the printed edition (with accurate KFM patterns) may be easy to get locally.The 1987 edition of Nuclear War Survival Skills includes the author's personal view that small radiation doses are healthful; FEMA, EPA and CDC do not accept that. Follow the government guidance in this folder for dose decisions.

🔧 Engines, Motors and Generators How to keep small gas engines, chainsaws and generators running, how to test and rebuild electric motors, and how to turn motors and car alternators into generators for charging batteries. The full shop manuals are in Engines-Motors\ (Small-Engines, Chainsaws-and-Saws, Electric-Motors, Motors-as-Generators). Creek hydro and solar are in Off-Grid-Power\; electricity basics are in the Navy NEETS modules there. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never run an engine or generator indoors, in a garage, shed or crawlspace — carbon monoxide kills in minutes, even with doors open. - Never refuel a hot or running engine. Keep the can touching the tank while pouring (stops static sparks). - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding") — use a transfer switch or interlock. It can kill someone working on the lines. - Capacitors bite. Motor capacitors (and microwave ovens) can hold a deadly charge after unplugging. Discharge across the terminals with an insulated screwdriver or a resistor before touching. - Pull the spark plug wire before working on a mower blade, saw chain or anything the engine turns.

⛽ Small gas engines: why it won't start Every engine needs three things: compression, spark and fuel. Find which one is missing. (MAVCC Small Engine Repair) 1. Fuel: pull the plug, cover the hole with a finger and pull the starter 2–3 times. A wet finger means fuel is arriving. If dry, check: fuel in the tank, shutoff valve open, cap vent not blocked, carburetor bowl (drain it — water or gum?), fuel filter and line. 2. Spark: put a spare plug on the plug wire, rest it against the metal head and crank. A bright blue spark is good. Yellow, weak or none = clean or replace the plug, check the kill-switch wire, then the coil/magneto. 3. Compression: spin the flywheel backward against compression — a sharp rebound is good. Weak = loose plug or head, stuck valve, worn rings. Old fuel is the #1 problem. Gas goes stale in about 60 days without stabilizer (sooner with ethanol). For longer storage, drain the tank and run the carburetor dry, or add stabilizer and run it a few minutes so it reaches the carburetor. Keep cans sealed — water in ethanol gas separates and ruins engines. (Oklahoma Extension BAE-1746) Cleaning a carburetor (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2): - Take a photo before you take it apart. Soak metal parts several hours in carb cleaner, then blow out every passage with

a carburetor (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2): - Take a photo before you take it apart. Soak metal parts several hours in carb cleaner, then blow out every passage with air. - Plastic or nylon parts no more than 30 minutes; never soak cork or coated floats. - Don't poke jets with wire — it enlarges them. Use a bristle, fishing line or air. - Always fit new gaskets. Float too high = floods; too low = starves. Two-stroke fuel (chainsaws, trimmers): mix oil at the ratio printed on the engine or in its manual. Never run straight gas — it seizes the engine in minutes. Rule of thumb: most modern saws are 50:1 (about 2.6 oz of 2-stroke oil per gallon); older gear is often 16:1–32:1. Don't mix mineral and synthetic 2-stroke oils. Routine care: check oil every use (4-strokes), clean the air filter often (a choked filter makes an engine run rich and weak), keep cooling fins clear, replace the plug yearly.

🪚 Chainsaws, crosscut saws and axes - A sharp chain throws chips; a dull one makes dust — and dust clogs the filter and raises kickback risk. (USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course) - Filing: use the file size for your chain, with a guide. Hold the file level with about one-fifth of it above the cutter's top plate, guide mark parallel to the chain. File from the inside of each cutter outward, all of one side, then turn the saw around. Keep all cutters the same length. - Depth gauges (the little humps in front of each cutter): check with a gauge tool every few sharpenings, file down only to the tool, and round off the front. - Running out of fuel isn't the end of cutting. A sharp crosscut saw and ax still fell and buck trees. Raker depth for a crosscut: 0.008 in for hard, dry wood up to 0.030 in for soft, springy wood; start at about 0.012 in. (USFS Crosscut Saw Manual, Saws That Sing, An Ax to Grind)

🔋 Generators - Maintenance: oil change every 50–100 hours (sooner when new), clean air filter, fresh or stabilized fuel, run it under load for 20–30 minutes once a month. - Load: add up the running watts of what you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2–3× their running watts for a second). Keep steady load under about 80% of the generator's rating. - Grounding: follow the generator's own manual. (The Army 3 kW set procedure is a ground rod at least 8 ft deep with No. 6 copper wire — TM 5-6115-271-14.) - No output but the engine runs? Check the breaker on the generator, then the brushes and voltage regulator (most small generators). A generator that sat unused can lose its residual magnetism — see "flashing the field" below.

⚙️ Electric motors: testing and repair Single-phase motor hums but won't start (pumps, compressors, shop tools): suspect the start capacitor or the centrifugal start switch, which should click open at about ¾ speed. Discharge the capacitor, check it (a bulged or leaking one is dead; a meter with a capacitance setting tells for sure), and replace with the same microfarads and same or higher voltage. (TM 5-683; Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use) Basic winding checks with a meter (Navy Electrician's Mate): - Windings must have no opens (infinite ohms through a winding), no shorts (much lower reading than its twin), and no grounds (any reading from a winding to the frame). - The three windings of a 3-phase motor should read nearly the same resistance. - Insulation test (megger): right after shutdown while warm and dry, with capacitors disconnected. At least 0.5 megohm for motors 250 V and under, 1 megohm up to 1000 V. (TM 5-683) - Armatures (brushed motors): test bar-to-bar on the commutator with a low-ohm meter; a "growler" finds shorted coils (a hacksaw blade buzzes over the bad coil). Bearings: a rumbling or hot bearing is the most common motor failure. Replace with the same number stamped on it. Fit new bearings by heating them to about 200 °F (oil bath or oven, not a flame). Never wash sealed bearings in solvent. Brushes and commutators

number stamped on it. Fit new bearings by heating them to about 200 °F (oil bath or oven, not a flame). Never wash sealed bearings in solvent. Brushes and commutators (drills, saws, mixers, car starters, DC motors): replace brushes before they're shorter than about ¼ in. Seat new brushes by pulling fine sandpaper (grit toward the brush) under them around the commutator, then blow out the carbon dust. A blackened, grooved commutator can be cleaned with a commutator stone or fine sandpaper, or turned lightly on a lathe (no more than 0.010 in per cut). Rewinding a burned motor (Braymer & Roe Rewinding Small Motors; DOE Repair Specifications): - Before stripping, record everything: turns per coil, wire size, coil span (slots), how coils connect, and lead markings. Photograph each step. - Strip old windings at no more than about 680 °F (360 °C) or the iron core is damaged. - Rewind with the same total copper area per turn and same turns (two thinner wires in parallel can replace one thick one). Varnish and bake below about 195 °F to dry. - Small burned motors are often easier to replace from salvage than to rewind — keep a stock.

🔁 Motors as generators What works best, easiest first: 1. Permanent-magnet DC motors (treadmill motors, wheelchair, scooter, some cordless tool motors): spin them and they make DC directly. Output voltage rises with speed, so choose one that makes at least 14–15 V at the speed you can actually turn it to charge a 12 V battery. Add a blocking diode so the battery can't run it as a motor. (Rule of thumb) 2. Car alternators: built-in rectifier and regulator, but they need about 1,500+ rpm (step-up pulleys or belts for wind, water or pedals) and a battery connected to power their field — they are not self-starting. The field draws about 3 A, which wastes a lot at low power. (ED021119 Alternator and Regulator Servicing) 3. Induction motors (ordinary AC motors) as generators: drive it faster than its synchronous speed by about as much as its rated slip — e.g. a motor rated 1725 rpm (1800 synchronous) is driven at about 1875 rpm. On its own (not tied to the grid) it needs capacitors across the windings to excite it. (DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 2, in Off-Grid-Power\Micro-Hydro) - Rule of thumb: start with run capacitors whose current at rated voltage roughly matches the motor's no-load current, then trim until voltage and frequency are right. Use AC motor-run (film) capacitors, never electrolytic start capacitors. - Expect about 70–80% of the motor's

roughly matches the motor's no-load current, then trim until voltage and frequency are right. Use AC motor-run (film) capacitors, never electrolytic start capacitors. - Expect about 70–80% of the motor's rating as output. Needs a ballast (dump) load or controller so voltage doesn't swing as loads switch. Aging capacitors make frequency creep up; a capacitor running hotter than the others is failing. (Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M) 4. Build a permanent-magnet alternator from magnets and magnet wire for a wind turbine or slow water wheel — full plans in Hugh Piggott's Axial Flux Alternator and PMG Construction Manual. Rules for any homemade generator: - Never let a wind or water generator run with no load — it overspeeds and can destroy itself. Use a diversion (dump-load) charge controller, not a solar controller (solar controllers disconnect the source). (DFID-ITDG Small Wind Systems) - Flashing the field: if a generator or self-excited induction generator won't build up voltage, touch a 12 V battery briefly across one field or winding to restore residual magnetism, then try again. (Rule of thumb) - Old method: the 1939 North Dakota circular shows turning a car generator into a 6-volt wind charger, and the DOE Wind Power for Farms handbook covers matching any generator to a rotor.Measurements and settings in old manuals are fine for methods; for your specific engine, motor or generator, its own nameplate and manual

Farms handbook covers matching any generator to a rotor.Measurements and settings in old manuals are fine for methods; for your specific engine, motor or generator, its own nameplate and manual come first.

💊 Using found or expired medicines 1. Identify it. US pills must carry an imprint code. Open Pill-Identifier\PILL-IDENTIFIER.html, type the code, then check that the color, shape and size also match — the same code can be two different drugs (e.g. "I2" is ibuprofen 200 mg or amitriptyline 25 mg depending on size; "N 4" is nitroglycerin or a diet pill). No code at all = a supplement, a foreign or compounded product, or an illegal pill. 2. Never trust street pills. Pills that didn't come from a pharmacy can be counterfeits pressed with fentanyl — fake blue "M30" oxycodone, Xanax and Adderall are common, and many contain a deadly dose. 3. Look it up before giving it. In the WHO Model Formulary or MSF Essential Drugs (Medicines\), read what it treats, the dose, who must not take it, and interactions. For children, use the WHO Formulary for Children — children's doses go by weight. 4. Expired medicines. Most tablets and capsules kept sealed, cool and dry lose potency slowly — military testing extended most stockpiled lots by years, and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date. But: - Don't rely on expired or badly stored: insulin (lasts only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin tablets (lose strength once opened — keep in the original glass bottle), epinephrine pens (weaker when expired — but an
